name: Davy's Grey
lede: Davy's Grey is a neutral, mid-dark grey from Robert Ridgway's 1912 color dictionary, and its hex value is within half a unit of the Inter-Society Color Council's own definition of dark gray.

sections.title: A surname, unexplained
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 “Color Standards and Color Nomenclature” lists Davy's Grey at hex #555555 among the names he credits to a person [1]. Ridgway does not give a first name or a reason for the name, so whether it honors a particular Davy, as some painters' color names do for a pigment maker or a colorist, is undocumented in our sources [1]. The 1955 Inter-Society Color Council catalog repeats the name, and that circular's block for dark gray matches this swatch within 0.4 color-difference units, closer than almost any other name in our library [1].

Its nearest neighbor in our color graph is [[vienna-smoke|Vienna Smoke]], only 2.7 units away and almost the same [1]. [[greyish-black|Greyish Black]] and [[pelican|Pelican]] sit almost as close [1]. Against the basic color words it reads closest to [[umber|Umber]], 9.6 units off, though Davy's Grey carries no warmth that umber has [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive matches this grey in 2.28% of 23,781 paintings, 543 of them, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 302 [2]. That makes it more common than 77% of the named colors in our set [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, present in 2.8% of the 1,674 paintings from that century, 1.9 times the rate its museums would predict [2]. Inside a painting it most often sits as a mid-tone, in 46% of its 302 appearances, by lightness rank rather than by brand [2]. Henri Matisse is its most devoted painter here, holding it in 5 of 50 works, 3.8 times the baseline of the museums those paintings come from [2]. Our earliest match dates to 1235, by the Master of the Bigallo Crucifix, 677 years before Ridgway's 1912 book recorded the name, a floor rather than a first, since a color match in an aged photograph is not proof of a pigment [2].
